title: Many rites (CCC 1200–1206)
hook: Latin, Byzantine, Alexandrian, Syriac, Armenian, Maronite, Chaldean: one faith, many forms

segments.voice: Yesterday, the church building, and the ambo, where the word of God is proclaimed. Your line was each place speaks. Did you find the ambo and the font, in a real church or a remembered one? Day one thousand ninety-three.

Two Catholic churches, one Sunday morning, a few streets apart. In the first, the priest stands at a plain altar facing the people, and an organ plays. In the second, painted icons stretch across the front, incense hangs in the air, and nearly everything is sung, back and forth between the priest and the people. The prayers are different. The vestments are different. Even the name is different: in the second church people may call it the Divine Liturgy. Yet both communities are Catholic, both are in communion with the Pope, and both celebrate the same Eucharist. How can that be? Today's word answers it.
screen: `TWO CHURCHES, ONE SUNDAY.` → `ORGAN HERE, ICONS AND INCENSE THERE.` → `BOTH CATHOLIC.`

segments.voice: The word is rite. In ordinary speech a rite is a ceremony. In the Catechism it means something bigger: a whole family of worship, with its own prayers, music, calendar and way of doing things, handed down in a particular part of the Church. The Catechism starts with what doesn't change. It's the one mystery of Christ, his death and resurrection, that the Church celebrates everywhere. Then it makes a striking claim: that mystery is so rich that no single liturgical tradition can say all of it. So, as the Gospel traveled, it took root among different peoples, and their worship grew in harmony with their languages and cultures. The Catechism names the traditions in use today. The Latin, which is mainly the Roman rite and also some local and religious-order rites. The Byzantine. The Alexandrian, or Coptic. The Syriac. The Armenian. The Maronite. The Chaldean. Repeating the Second Vatican Council, it says the Church holds all lawfully recognized rites to be of equal right and dignity, and wants to keep them alive and growing. Not a main rite and some exotic extras. Equal. But the Catechism also sets a limit. Diversity mustn't damage unity. The rites stay one by keeping the same apostolic faith, the same sacraments, and communion with the bishops and the Pope. So the icons and the organ aren't rivals. They're two ways of saying one thing. Each is fully at home in the one Church.
screen: `A RITE: A WHOLE FAMILY OF WORSHIP.` · `ONE MYSTERY, TOO RICH FOR ONE FORM.` · `EQUAL RIGHT AND DIGNITY.` · `DIVERSITY MUST NOT HARM UNITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn about one rite. Settle, and breathe. Let the names go by slowly, one for each breath. Latin. Byzantine. Alexandrian. Syriac. Armenian. Maronite. Chaldean. Notice which one you know least about. That's the one to learn about later today: what language its liturgy uses, or what its churches look like, or whether there's a parish of that rite anywhere near you. For now, just hold the name. If you pray, you can hold up the Catholics of that rite, wherever they are. The bell holds the time.
Rite. Not one ceremony but a whole tradition of worship, with its own prayers and ways, celebrating the one mystery of Christ. Today's word.
Your line: one faith, many forms. Today, find one photograph or recording of a liturgy in a rite you've never seen, and stay with it for a minute. Day one thousand ninety-three.

howItsDone: Roman-rite parishes celebrate the Mass, while Byzantine Catholic parishes celebrate what they call the Divine Liturgy; each Eastern Catholic church keeps its own liturgy, calendar and customs.
